name: AI in Education
blurb: Artificial intelligence is already in schools, in the tools teachers plan with, the software students practise on, and the systems that run buses and budgets. These pages, built on the book The AI Ready School, set out what works from preschool to graduation, what the evidence shows, and the rule that runs through all of it: AI may inform a decision about a child, but a named person makes it.

children.name: Getting Oriented
children.blurb: The first four chapters lay the foundation for everything that follows. They explain what AI can and cannot do, the ten patterns that account for nearly every idea in the Volume, the laws and rules that protect students, and a simple method for piloting and measuring any new tool.

children.name: The Classroom
children.blurb: Part II, The Classroom, covers AI in each stage and subject. It begins with preschool through second grade, then turns to reading and writing, mathematics, science and computing, social studies and world languages, the arts and physical education, and personalized learning and tutoring.

children.name: Every Student, Every Family
children.blurb: Part III, Every Student, Every Family, covers special education and accessibility, English learners and newcomers, communication with families, wellbeing and safety, and counseling and college. These chapters address the students and families who most need careful attention.

children.name: Running the School
children.blurb: Part IV, Running the School, covers teacher planning and grading, assessment and data, operations and finance, and people and leadership. These chapters speak most directly to principals, district leaders, and board members.

sections.body: This part of school life is about AI in education, where a school does not only use AI to run operations but is responsible for what AI does to how children learn and for protecting children while it happens. The book describes AI arriving in schools faster than almost any technology before it, with students finding free chat tools before most districts had a policy and teachers using AI to plan lessons before anyone trained them. It says the same kind of tool can help students learn or keep them from learning, and the outcome depends on how adults design and supervise its use. The Volume gathers 300 practical ideas across 20 chapters, from preschool through graduation and from the classroom to the business office. Every idea carries an evidence label, and the labels are honest about how young the field is and how much weight each idea can bear.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The book finds that AI tutoring works when teachers design and supervise it, as in after school sessions where teachers wrote the opening prompt and stayed in the room, and that plain chatbot practice without that supervision harmed later exam scores because students copied answers. It also finds that weekly messages to families about missed work, grades, and absences cut course failures, that plain supportive notices outperformed legal language, and that personal reminders from a student's own counselor helped students reach college while national campaigns had no effect. What does not work or is not yet known includes AI detectors that misclassify writing by students still learning English, no evidence that online monitoring prevents harm, no independent evaluation of AI security systems in schools, and thin research on young children and students with disabilities. The rules it holds to are that people make every decision affecting a student, student names and details stay out of any tool without a signed data privacy agreement, tools give hints rather than answers, every AI draft is checked by a person, and every flag leads to a person who reaches out. The core argument is that adoption fails when leaders mandate tools they do not use, reward logins instead of results, and skip the rules, and it succeeds when leaders model use, measure hours saved and student outcomes, and publish the rules for privacy, review, and accountability.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The pages fit together as a path from Getting Oriented, which gives the volume's purpose, its four audiences, its evidence labels, and its five rules, to The Classroom, to Every Student, Every Family, and then to Running the School. The Classroom is for teachers who need practical ideas for planning, teaching, feedback, and grading, organized by subject and grade. Every Student, Every Family speaks to parents and to anyone who wants to know how children are using AI and whether the school is protecting them, including five questions every parent should be able to ask a school. Running the School is for principals, district leaders, and school board members who need guidance on policy, pilots, purchasing, professional learning, and the questions and evidence a board should expect. The final chapter lays out the first 90 days for a superintendent, a principal, a teacher, and a parent, and none of those steps requires buying anything.
